{{Short description|Mathematical theorem about Banach spaces}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=July 2026}}
In the [[mathematics|mathematical]] theory of [[Banach space]]s, the '''closed range theorem''' gives necessary and sufficient conditions for a [[closed linear operator|closed]] [[densely defined operator]] to have [[closed set|closed]] [[range of a function|range]].

The theorem was proved by [[Stefan Banach]] in his 1932 ''[[Théorie des opérations linéaires]]''.  

== Statement ==

Let <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math> be Banach spaces, <math>T : D(T) \to Y</math> a closed linear operator whose domain <math>D(T)</math> is dense in <math>X,</math> and <math>T'</math> the [[Unbounded_operator#Transpose|transpose]] of <math>T</math>. The theorem asserts that the following conditions are equivalent:

* <math>R(T),</math> the range of <math>T,</math> is closed in <math>Y.</math>
* <math>R(T'),</math> the range of <math>T',</math> is closed in <math>X',</math> the [[continuous dual space|dual]] of <math>X.</math>
* <math>R(T) = N(T')^\perp = \left\{  y \in Y  : \langle x^*,y \rangle = 0 \quad {\text{for all}}\quad x^* \in N(T') \right\}.</math>
* <math>R(T') = N(T)^\perp  = \left\{x^* \in X' : \langle x^*,y \rangle = 0 \quad {\text{for all}}\quad y \in N(T) \right\}.</math>

Where <math>N(T)</math> and <math>N(T')</math> are the null space of <math>T</math> and <math>T'</math>, respectively.

Note that there is always an inclusion <math>R(T)\subseteq N(T')^\perp</math>, because if <math>y=Tx</math> and <math>x^*\in N(T')</math>, then <math>\langle x^*,y\rangle = \langle T'x^*,x\rangle = 0</math>.  Likewise, there is an inclusion <math>R(T')\subseteq N(T)^\perp</math>.  So the non-trivial part of the above theorem is the opposite inclusion in the final two bullets.

== Corollaries ==

Several corollaries are immediate from the theorem.  For instance, a densely defined closed operator <math>T</math> as above has <math>R(T) = Y</math> if and only if the transpose <math>T'</math> has a continuous inverse.  Similarly, <math>R(T') = X'</math> if and only if <math>T</math> has a continuous inverse.

== Sketch of proof ==
Since the graph of ''T'' is closed, the proof reduces to the case when <math>T : X \to Y</math> is a bounded operator between Banach spaces. Now, <math>T</math> factors as <math>X \overset{p}\to X/\operatorname{ker}T \overset{T_0}\to \operatorname{im}T \overset{i}\hookrightarrow Y</math>. Dually, <math>T'</math> is
:<math>Y' \to (\operatorname{im}T)' \overset{T_0'}\to (X/\operatorname{ker}T)' \to X'.</math>
Now, if <math> \operatorname{im}T</math> is closed, then it is Banach and so by the [[open mapping theorem (functional analysis)|open mapping theorem]], <math>T_0</math> is a topological isomorphism. It follows that <math>T_0'</math> is an isomorphism and then <math>\operatorname{im}(T') = \operatorname{ker}(T)^{\bot}</math>. (More work is needed for the other implications.<!-- and we should add proofs for those too. -->) <math>\square</math>
